paras: The whitecapping of Fleming Brown was a night visit by a neighbors' "committee of safety" to the home of Fleming Brown, a Black man living near Ashby in the Cumberland, Virginia, neighborhood, in late spring 1903. The band, which a Washington paper called "Whitecaps," reportedly made Brown "pay well" for allegedly beating his young ward after a court had declined to take her from his care.

Fleming and Amanda Brown, described as "colored," were guardians of Rosa Taylor, a sixteen-year-old girl the dispatch called a "dwarf" and "stunted and weakly." Several weeks before the dispatch, according to the report, her guardian beat her so badly that her garments were "cemented to her skin with her own blood," and the marks stayed visible for nine days. Neighbors who heard the girl's account took the case to court, but the Browns kept custody, and the court instructed them "to whip her when she needed it, but not cruelly."

The ruling, the dispatch said, made the neighbors "determined to take the matter in their hands," and they organized a "committee of safety." At 1 a.m. "one morning recently," the committee went to the Browns' house near Ashby, and it was reported that its members "made Fleming Brown pay well for his cruelty." The dispatch did not say what was done to Brown, how many men took part, or whether Amanda Brown was harmed.
The dispatch closed by noting that the committee "have several other matters to look into." No report of arrests, an investigation or any court action against the committee appears in the coverage.

The only account found is a special dispatch, datelined Cumberland, Va., June 5, and sent through Richmond, that ran in the Washington Evening Star on June 5, 1903, under the headline "WHITE CAPS IN VIRGINIA. Court's Decision in Cruelty Case Causes Action." The Evening Star framed the visit as a consequence of the court's ruling, gave most of its space to the girl's injuries, and described the punishment as making Brown "pay well for his cruelty," without criticizing the band. No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

accounts.label: Special dispatch (Cumberland, Va., via Richmond)
accounts.gist: After a court left the dwarf girl Rosa Taylor with her 'colored' guardians despite an alleged severe beating, neighbors formed a 'committee of safety' that went to the Browns' house at 1 a.m. and reportedly made Fleming Brown 'pay well for his cruelty'.

framing.detail: Headlined 'WHITE CAPS IN VIRGINIA', the dispatch treats the night visit as a consequence of the 'Court's Decision in Cruelty Case', dwells on the girl's injuries, and reports the punishment sympathetically ('pay well for his cruelty') without condemning the band.
